Tech stocks were mixed Tuesday afternoon, with the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) fractionally lower and the State Street SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (XSD) adding 0.7%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor index increased 0.2%.

In corporate news, Salesforce (CRM) agreed to buy customer engagement platform Braze (BRZE) in a deal worth $5.66 billion, as it looks to strengthen its business-to-consumer marketing solutions. Shareholders of Braze's class A stock will receive $47.50 in cash per share, the companies said. Salesforce shares were up 0.1%, and Braze surged 51%.

Apple (AAPL) announced new and expanded partnerships with US suppliers to make key components for its iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro models under its American Manufacturing Program. Apple shares were down 0.5%.

IBM's (IBM) venture capital arm IBM Ventures has made a strategic investment in Leena AI, the agentic artificial intelligence company said Tuesday. The investment will support Leena's AI Colleague platform as clients move from AI assistants to autonomous AI agents for tasks in human resources, information technology and finance, according to a statement. IBM shares rose 1.5%.

llm-d 1.0 consolidates a hardened core for distributed inference validated for day 2 production deployments that helps organizations improve AI serving efficiency and scale enterprise workloads.

llm-d is broadly adopted and trusted by frontier model labs, hyperscalers and neoclouds, hardware accelerators, and major enterprises, with recent demonstrations showing up to five to 10 times cost reductions for context-heavy agentic workloads1 and three times greater output throughput.2

SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, llm-d project contributors announced the release of llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for the open source project designed to help organizations deploy and scale large language model inference more efficiently across modern infrastructure. Founded in 2025 by Red Hat, IBM (NYSE: IBM), Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production.

IBM Corporation logo.

As organizations race to put AI into production, many are discovering that running AI at scale can be as challenging and expensive as building the models themselves. Organizations need a way to deliver responsive experiences for users, support agentic workloads, and maximize utilization of increasingly scarce compute resources. llm-d 1.0 is built to address these challenges through intelligent distributed inference capabilities to facilitate improvements in performance, increases in throughput and help organizations gain greater control over the economics of AI serving.

Turning Innovation into Production Reality

With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI ROI. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference — across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang.

llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. title: What Could Derail Dell Stock?
detail:
What Could Derail Dell Stock?
Trefis Team
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 4:02 AM MST 4 min read
DELL
^GSPC
HPQ
HPE
IBM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Dell Technologies (DELL) stock returned 204.4% over the year to October 19, 2026, compared with a 17.4% return for the S&P 500. Buyers at the current price are paying for Dell's sales growth to continue. During a September 1 earnings call, management said that a shortage of parts, led by memory chips, still limits the business, and it was asked on the same call how solid the growth really is. So what is that problem, and why does it raise doubts about the growth?

A Memory Chip Shortage Is Raising Dell's Costs

Dell cannot get all the memory chips it wants. On the September 1 call, management said the constraints remain unchanged: DRAM first, followed by NAND, alongside spotty CPU shortages. These components also cost more, and management said its storage products cost more because of the cost basis of NAND.

Higher prices pose a more difficult question about the growth. On the same call, management was asked whether the growth comes from a mix of pricing and prebuys, with customers buying early, rather than real demand. Management said that customers are placing their orders further in advance to guarantee supply. Orders booked early to beat a shortage count today, but some of them may represent demand borrowed from later quarters, and that is the worry.

Management also heard the opposite concern on the call. It was asked how much demand is being deferred because customers cannot raise their budgets fast enough to keep up with the price increases. If customers are putting orders off, today's sales understate demand rather than overstate it.

How Much Of Dell's Business Does The Shortage Touch?

The shortage affects PCs, as Dell steered its memory supply away from them, and it impacts the Infrastructure Solutions Group. That division sells Dell's servers and storage, accounting for 53.6% of the company's revenue in fiscal 2026. The infrastructure business generated $60.8 billion in revenue, up 39.5% from the year before, while the Client Solutions Group grew 5.4%.

Within the infrastructure business, traditional server and networking revenue reached $10.5 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, up 122%, and management said demand continued to outpace supply. Earlier in fiscal 2027, when management saw signs that the PC market would soften in the second half, Dell steered its memory supply toward the infrastructure business.

Dell's stock price appears to assume that this growth continues. The company trades at 1.9 times its sales over the last twelve months, compared with 0.947 times at the end of September 2025. Over the past 32 quarter ends, the highest was 2.3 times on September 30, 2026. The shares have already retreated, closing 22.7% below their high of the past year on October 19.
